Flu activity has risen since May but remains below baseline; a summer peak is possible as activity increases. The current influenza positivity rate is 4.11%, up about 0.4 percentage points from last week; wastewater surveillance also indicates increased activity. Last summer peak lasted September to January; there was no winter peak this year, so a summer peak could occur earlier than usual. COVID-19 has been active since May with potential dual peaks; vaccination is encouraged, noting uptake among children aged 6 months to 2 years is under 4%.

articleSummary: Brazilian Embrapa Pesca e Aquicultura (TO) and Italy's IZSVe developed a GIS-based early warning model to map infection risk for fish farms within the same hydrographic basin, focusing on the acanthocephalan parasite (acanthocephalan) in tambaqui (Colossoma macropomum). articleSummary: Kaohsiung, Taiwan — A nosocomial dengue cluster at Kaohsiung Municipal Minsheng Hospital reached six cases by June 15; as of June 16 no new cases. All cases are ward contacts of the index patient; viral sequencing matches a Vietnam-origin imported case (onset June 1), with no wider transmission and surveillance through July 12. The response includes 24 field deployments, hospital and community vector control, environmental cleanup, and expanded testing (~1,400 people), with only the six positives. Through June 15, Taiwan has 75 dengue cases: 7 locally in Kaohsiung and 68 imported from Southeast/South Asia (Indonesia 21, Maldives 14, Vietnam 9). Globally, dengue surpassed 1.02 million by April, rising in Asia (Vietnam, Malaysia, Sri Lanka) and the Americas (Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia). Public guidance urges eliminating standing water (sweep, drain, clean, scrub) and using repellents with DEET, Picaridin, or IR-3535; febrile travelers should seek prompt care.

articleSummary: Two Vietnamese workers returning from Africa were hospitalized with malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum. The cases were reported on 16 June 2026. The first patient, a 36-year-old man from Thanh Hóa who worked in the Congo, had repeated malaria episodes during his stay and developed fever near 40°C, rigors, headache, nausea, and dizziness two weeks after returning. The second patient, a 45-year-old man who worked in Angola, had malaria abroad and, after returning, two months later suffered a relapse with fever to 40.2°C, severe chills lasting about three hours, twice daily. Both tested positive for P. falciparum and were transferred for treatment. After receiving injectable and oral anti-malarials, both improved and stabilized. Doctors warn P. falciparum can cause severe illness and multi-organ failure if untreated; travelers from Africa should seek early medical testing and use protective measures against mosquitoes, and consult about prophylaxis.

articleSummary: As of 2026-06-16, a preprint by Japan’s National Institute of Infectious Diseases and the University of Tokyo estimates the risk of airborne importation of Ebola virus disease caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus during the Congo–Uganda outbreak via international air travel. The study used May 2024 passenger data (11,264 airports, 569,741 routes, >329 million travelers) and Ndjili International Airport in Kinshasa as the outbreak’s origin to compute an “effective distance” between airports and the probability of at least one importation within 30 days. In the main model, Belgium 77.7%, France 77.5%, South Africa 75.3%; upper-bound estimates: Belgium 92.0%, France 91.9%, South Africa 90.5%. Other top destinations: Kenya, United Arab Emirates, Turkey, Uganda, India, Ivory Coast, Canada; Turkey 69.8% main, 86.7% upper; Canada 64.2% main, 82.3% upper. Congo outbreak had 192 deaths and >808 confirmed cases; WHO declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern with high regional risk.

articleSummary: Two Vietnamese workers returning from Africa were diagnosed with malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, the most dangerous malaria parasite. The cases involve Congo and Angola. Symptoms included high fever with severe chills, headaches, nausea, and dizziness; one patient had recurring febrile episodes during his Congo assignment. Both received intensive treatment with antimalarials via injections and oral routes, with good response; fever resolved and health improving under monitoring. articleSummary: Malaria is confirmed again in Kozhikode district, Kerala, as of 2026-06-16. An Olavanna resident, a 63-year-old headload worker, was hospitalized at Beach Hospital after persistent fever and malaria was confirmed by testing. In the same district, in Thikkod, a guest worker from Madhya Pradesh was diagnosed with malaria and is being treated at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes; five human parasites exist, with Plasmodium falciparum the most dangerous and common, while P. vivax can relapse. articleSummary: On June 16, 2026, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) extends to Mongbwalu in Ituri province, the epicentre of the 17th outbreak. An Ebola Treatment Center operated by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is now at Mongbwalu General Hospital, with 18 laboratory-confirmed cases receiving care. A diagnostic lab on site, installed about 10 days earlier, has sharply reduced turnaround times; previously samples were sent to Bunia and Kinshasa, roughly 3,000 km away. The response faces distrust and violence: initial tents were burned, NGO vehicles vandalized, and staff threatened; community acceptance is growing but resistance remains. Red Cross burials report 7–10 deaths daily in Mongbwalu, with many corpses abandoned or not handled under safe conditions. Mongbwalu's forest setting, artisanal gold mining zones, and armed-group–controlled areas complicate access and transmission interruption, with all alerts routed through local health zones.

articleSummary: Malaria has been confirmed again in Kozhikode district, Kerala, with a 63-year-old Olavanna resident currently hospitalized at Beach Hospital after fever prompted diagnostic testing. articleHeadline: Canada, Japan Forge Zoning Pact for Swine Fever Defense
articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) zoning pact between Canada and Japan ensures pork exports from ASF-free zones to Japan even if ASF is present elsewhere in Canada. Canada remains ASF-free; ASF is highly contagious and fatal for pigs but not a risk to human health or food safety. The agreement preserves access to a key market, with Japan importing about $1.8 billion in pork and pork products in 2025, representing 31% of Canada’s total pork export value. With Japan, Canada now has ASF zoning arrangements in eight markets: United States, European Union, Singapore, Hong Kong, Vietnam, United Arab Emirates, Philippines, and Japan, collectively about 69% of Canada’s pork export value. The arrangement supports a science-based, internationally recognized approach to safe trade during an outbreak, mitigating market disruption while protecting animal health and food security.

articleSummary: Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite behind Chagas disease, shows silent circulation in dogs in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil. A Fiocruz-led study tested 290 dogs across three socially vulnerable neighborhoods and found 5.1% positive in Alto do Cabrito and Marechal Rondon, while Pau da Lima had no positives. The findings, published in Acta Tropica, suggest dogs can serve as sentinels for human risk in areas with poor sanitation and environmental conditions favorable to vectors, though authors caution the results are preliminary and do not confirm active transmission. Transmission to humans occurs mainly via triatomine bug feces; other routes include blood transfusion, organ transplant, contaminated food, and maternal/fetal transfer, with no documented direct dog-to-human transmission. Chagas manifests acutely for 3–8 weeks, and chronically affects heart, esophagus, or intestines; diagnosis relies on blood tests and phase-specific methods, with imaging used in chronic cases.

articleSummary: Public health drill in Hong Kong code-named 'Purple Dragon Crystal' strengthens inter-departmental response to suspected Ebola virus disease importations. Port Health staff coordinated medical assessment, infection control, environmental disinfection, and epidemiological investigation, then transferred the suspected case to the Hospital Authority Infectious Disease Centre at Queen Mary Hospital for isolation and treatment. The second part tested the Infectious Disease Centre’s capacity for isolation, infection control, critical care, and rapid viral testing. About 80 representatives from Fire Services, Airport Authority, and Hospital Authority participated. A suspected patient was transported to the Infectious Disease Centre. HK has conducted 33 similar drills for diseases including measles, plague, MERS, and avian influenza. Ebola is a filovirus; human-to-human transmission via infected fluids; CFR historically 25–90%, average ~50%. In May, WHO reported Bundibugyo Ebola outbreaks in DRC and Uganda; HK activated the lowest alert level and issued a red travel warning for DRC on May 21.
